Therefore, the conventional truth of dependent origination refutes that which is a truly existent nature.
Fourth, the worldly truth refutes the real.
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refutes the conventional (saṃvṛti). This has been explained as before.
Question: If the conventional truth refutes the real, then the conventional truth itself must be false.
If the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) were to negate the conventional (saṃvṛti), then the ultimate truth itself would not be conventional.
Answer: The ultimate truth negates the arising and ceasing of the conventional;
it does not say that the ultimate truth negates all conventionalities whatsoever.

Question: Since there are already four permutations (catuṣkoṭi), why is it now said that the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) refutes the real and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) refutes the provisional?
Answer: In general discussion, the provisional and the real do indeed comprise all four permutations.
Now, wishing to explain that both truths are devoid of arising:
thus, in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there is no real arising;
in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is no nominal arising.
Therefore, the two truths can be distinguished by their respective non-arising:
if one says that conventional truth negates actual arising,
while ultimate truth negates actual non-arising.
If one refutes arising and further refutes non-arising,
one fails to explain the "eight negations.
Therefore, the two truths cannot both be used to refute reality.
If conventional truth negates arising through designation,
and ultimate truth negates arising through designation,
this would likewise not be an explanation of the meaning of the "Eight Negations."
Therefore, it is not possible for both to refute the conventional.
If the conventional truth refutes conventional arising,
then the ultimate truth refutes substantial non-arising.
Nor does it explain the "Eight Negations.
Therefore, within the four gates, it merely attains the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) by clarifying that there is no real arising,
and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) by discerning that there is no provisional arising.
Question: Is it not the case that even the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) refutes actual arising?
Answer: If one grasps the intended meaning, it is indeed so;
for the conceptualization of "actual non-arising" is itself an attainment (*upalambha*).
This is merely the meaning of "arising. However,
since the opponent establishes their position from a superficial perspective and does not speak of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as being subject to arising,
the ultimate truth does not undermine arising.

Next, regarding "neither eternal nor discontinuous": having heard that in the True Dharma there is neither arising nor ceasing, one has from the outset maintained that the True Dharma possesses the principle of the four negations as its natural state;
whether a Buddha appears or not, the characteristics of its nature remain eternally constant, and for this reason it is eternal.
Yet the ultimate truth transcends the four propositions;
this is precisely what constitutes "cessation.
Now, in order to refute these views of annihilation and permanence, it is said that there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
Because this ultimate truth is not fixed as existing, it is not eternal;
because there has never been a fourfold proposition (catuṣkoṭi) that could be severed, it is called non-interruption.
This is termed the Middle Way.
Regarding "neither identical nor different":
when those who are deluded hear that there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilation nor permanence,
they then claim that the principle of ultimate truth is without differentiation.
Therefore, it is called "one.
One opens up and skillfully employs this.
Guangzhai [Master] claimed that because true reality also possesses degrees of depth, the various stages are separated by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, they are called "different.
Now, both are refuted;
hence it is said that they are neither identical nor different.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Without color and without form, it is a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of non-characteristic.
Because it is a single characteristic, it cannot be differentiated."
Because it is without marks (*animitta*), it cannot be said to be one.
That which is neither one nor different is called the Middle Way.
As for "neither coming nor going," this means that by the cessation of the conventional, the ultimate is attained.
Therefore it is called "coming.
Emerging from the ultimate truth into the mundane world is designated as "going forth."
Now, because this [objection] has been refuted and [the truth] has emerged, it is clearly shown that there is neither coming nor going.
Question: Where is this explanation made?
Answer: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the commentary on the "Chapter on Accumulation and Dispersion" (*Saṃcaya-vyavakiraṇa-parivarta*).
Regarding the statement that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) have accumulation and dispersal:
when one penetrates material objects and realizes emptiness,
this is the accumulation of the unconditioned.
To obstruct things and lose emptiness is the dispersion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This gathering and dispersing is precisely the meaning of coming and going.
Furthermore, it is because emptiness and form cannot be one.
Space does not emerge from within form,
for space and form cannot be differentiated.
Space does not come from outside form.
"Not coming and not going" constitutes the Middle Way within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

A question is raised: if "not arising and not ceasing" constitutes the Middle Way within the ultimate truth based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of provisional arising and ceasing, then may it also be said that "neither cutting off nor permanence" constitutes the Middle Way within the ultimate truth based on the conventional truth of provisional annihilation and permanence?
The answer is that this applies by analogy.
However, while the disciples of the Buddha accept that conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is subject to arising and ceasing,
they avoid [the extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism regarding conventional truth.
Therefore, it is not a mere analogy.
The concepts of identity and difference, as well as coming and going, can be applied to both meanings.
Furthermore, the two truths together possess the eight negations.
Regarding the unification of the Middle Way of the Two Truths, there are two meanings:
first, to explain the Middle Way by synthesizing the discussion of the Two Truths;
second, to dissolve the duality and return to non-duality, thereby discerning it within the essence.
Furthermore, there are three meanings regarding the synthesis of the two truths as the Middle Way.
First, when one intends to explain the meaning of the two truths as set forth in the sūtras and śāstras,
the scope of phenomena subsumed within these two truths is already exhaustive.
It is not necessary to clarify the three truths.
Second, there is the single clarification of the two truths;
this is the single clarification of the application of the Middle Way.
The first two clarify the Middle Way through the synthesis of the two truths;
the third clarifies that which is neither true nor conventional as being the Middle Way in terms of essence.
This explains the meaning of the three truths within the Sūtra.
Question: Why is it said that clarifying only the two truths constitutes the Middle Way?
Answer: This refers to the traditional meaning of the Middle Way regarding the two truths held by the Shadow Masters (Yingshi) within the Guanzhong school.
They state:
From the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no existence; from the perspective of conventional truth, there is no non-existence.
Although there is no existence from the perspective of ultimate truth, it exists despite being nonexistent.
Because it is conventional, non-existence is non-existent; though existence exists, it is non-existent.
Though non-existent, it exists, yet it does not stagnate in non-existence.
Though existent, it is non-existent, yet it is not burdened by existence.
Because it does not stagnate in non-existence,
it is not annihilated;
because it is not encumbered by existence, it is not eternal.
This is precisely the Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent, neither annihilated nor eternal;
this explains the meaning of the four "neither-s.
This is because birth and permanence are [regarded as] existence.
This is because cessation and abandonment are non-existent.
Regarding "neither identical nor different," one should explain it by analogy with the preceding:
from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are not identical.
From the perspective of ultimate truth, they are not different;
from the perspective of the conventional, there is no unity.
Although they are different, they are one because of ultimate truth; although they are one, they are different because of the conventional.
Though they are different, they are one;
thus, one does not stagnate in difference.
Though they are one, they are different.
Therefore, one does not cling to the "one.
That which is neither one nor different is called the Middle Way.
Regarding the establishment through refutation, Kaishan asserts that the ultimate and the conventional are of one essence.
Therefore, it is called "one.
Longguang maintains that the ultimate and the conventional are distinct entities;
therefore, he calls them "different names."
Now, both [extremes] are rejected;
therefore, it is said that they are neither identical nor different.
This is why Vasubandhu, in his commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, elucidates ten kinds of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*).
Since identity and difference are two kinds of conceptual distraction,
we know that the ultimate and the conventional cannot be either identical or different.
The *Verses on the Two Truths* by the Great Master Fu of Dongyang states:
"The two truths are not dual;
they are eternally distinct yet never separate."
Sinking or floating according to whether they follow [the current] or not;
drifting or mooring with no place to moor.
Such people originally do not study or inquire.
One should further know that the two truths cannot be either identical or different;
how much less could those who investigate the sūtras and śāstras harbor fixed attachments?
That which neither comes nor goes does not come because it is empty according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
and it does not go because it exists according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
"Goes" is synonymous with "departs."
The above examples illustrate this.
Question: Having already clarified the Middle Way within each of the two truths, why is it explained again by combining the two truths?
The answer is: if one explains only the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and does not explain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one falls exclusively into the extreme of existence.
If one explains only the ultimate truth and does not explain the conventional truth, [one likewise falls into the extreme of non-existence].
This would result in falling exclusively into the extreme of emptiness.
Now, by clarifying that the two truths are united and free from these two extremes,
it is called the Middle Way.
Dharma Master Dailang taught the two truths to Zhou Yong.
That person authored the *Treatise on the Three Tenets*, in which he states:
"The reason the Buddha established the two truths is..."
Because all phenomena possess both emptiness and existence,
they are not one-sided; therefore,
it is called the Middle Way.
Question: The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) transcends substantiality, and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) transcends the provisional.
When these two truths are explained together, what partiality do they remedy?

Answer: To clarify only that conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is devoid of intrinsic nature while failing to clarify that ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is devoid of the provisional is called "partial.
However, to clarify only that ultimate truth is devoid of the provisional while failing to clarify that conventional truth is devoid of intrinsic nature is also partial in its meaning.
Because the two truths are fully elucidated as both transcending the provisional and the real, the meaning is finally perfected and correct;
therefore, it is called the Middle Way.
Question: How are the two truths combined to elucidate the middle and the provisional?
Answer: To unify and clarify the two extremes as being non-dual constitutes the Middle Way.
Because it unifies and clarifies the causal conditions of the two truths, it is provisional.
Next, one dissolves the two truths.
Regarding the clarification of the Middle Way through returning to non-duality:
if one explains it in terms of essence and function, the first three types are all within the realm of function.
However, within this functioning, there are both separation and union.
To clarify the Middle Way within each of the two truths separately is to depart from them;
this is precisely to correctly establish the meaning of each of the two truths.
To clarify the Middle Way of the two truths together is to correctly unify the meaning of the two truths.
Now, clarifying that which is within the essence means gathering its functions back into the essence.
The reason this further stage is necessary is that those who receive the teachings hear it said that there are two truths.
Thus, forming two interpretations immediately constitutes two views.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"For all those who hold to duality, there is no Path and no fruit."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The wise and ignorance—fools call these two.
Likewise, the ultimate truth and the conventional—fools call these two."
Now, it is clarified that within the nameless and signless state of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, names and signs are provisionally established.
This teaching is intended to lead one to realize the nameless and signless by means of names and signs;
therefore, that which is non-dual yet divided into two is called the Two Truths.
Because it intends to cause one to awaken to both non-duality and duality through the non-dual,
it is called the Middle Way of Non-Duality.
It takes emptiness and existence as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is arising;
that which has emptiness as its essence is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The ultimate truth is termed cessation (*nirodha*).
Since it is called "empty" when there is existence, it is not existent;
therefore, it is said to be unarisen.
When there is emptiness within existence, that is not [true] emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that they are not extinguished.
Non-arising and non-extinction is precisely the Middle Way that is neither real nor conventional.
The principle of being neither permanent nor discontinuous may be understood by analogy with the above.
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the characteristics of the Buddha-nature are eternally present whether a Buddha appears or not;
therefore, it is called "constant.
In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all phenomena are merely provisional.
It must inevitably return to extinction;
therefore, it is called "annihilation.
Thus the Tathāgata speaks of these causes and conditions as both permanent and impermanent.
It is called the Middle Way because it causes sentient beings to realize that things are neither eternal nor impermanent; furthermore,
these terms may be explained in relation to one another.
When those who are deluded hear of the Middle Way— which is neither true nor mundane, and neither arising nor ceasing—
they take it to be eternal.
Since it is neither true nor mundane, they conclude that it transcends both the true and the mundane.
Therefore, it is called "cessation.
To bring this mind to rest,
one realizes that it is neither subject to arising and ceasing, nor to annihilation and permanence.
This is what is called the Middle Way.
Regarding "neither identical nor different":
if one follows the preceding principle, taking emptiness and existence as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is precisely non-differentiation and differentiation;
therefore, it is termed "identity and difference.
With emptiness (śūnyatā) as its essence, it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Ultimate truth is both differentiated and non-differentiated;
therefore, it is called "otherness-and-oneness.
This otherness-and-oneness is precisely not oneness.
Identity is precisely non-difference;
that which is neither different nor identical is called the Middle Way.
This is for the purpose of establishing what was stated above.
Those who are deluded, having heard that the Middle Way is neither arising nor ceasing, and neither eternal nor annihilated,
immediately claim it is a state of total obliteration into a single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
Yet, if one were to eliminate even this single mark, they would further claim that the Middle Way itself possesses degrees of depth.
This is precisely the characteristic of difference.
Because those whose minds grasp at something must necessarily have a basis;
if one does not abide in the "one," one then falls into "difference."
Therefore, it is now clarified that since [reality] is neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal,
it is likewise neither identical nor different.
As for "neither coming nor going," this is explained by analogy with the preceding [section], wherein emptiness and existence are established as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is coming;
from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is emptiness, there is cessation regarding all existent phenomena (*bhāva*).
Therefore, it is called "going."
The Tathāgata speaks of coming and going in order to bring about the realization that there is no coming and going.
Since "coming" is a coming characterized by non-coming,
what comes has nowhere from which to come.
Going is the characteristic of non-going, because going has no place to go.
Not coming and not going is called the Middle Way.
If one establishes this superior meaning, having heard the Middle Way, does it not possess the aforementioned six aspects?
One then claims that the Middle Way exists outside of the two extremes;
therefore, it is called "exiting.
If one previously clings to the two extremes, the Middle Way cannot be established.
Now, because the two extremes are abandoned, there is the Middle Way;
thus, the Middle Way is first established.
To still this mind, it is clarified that the Middle is neither an extreme nor something external.
Therefore, there is no emerging.
Since there is not even a limit from which to emerge,
how could there be a middle from which to come?
Question: For what reason is this explanation given?
Answer: The treatise states that these eight matters collectively refute all phenomena (*dharma*).
The "destruction of all phenomena" refers to the sequential deconstruction of the mental activities of sentient beings.
Since the minds of sentient beings operate solely within these eight matters,
they are now entirely negated.
It causes the mind to have no place of activity;
because there is no place of activity, there is nothing to be attained.
This is precisely the profound awakening to non-arising.
Therefore, this explanation is provided.

Next, to conclude: although there are four types, when combined through conventional designation (*prajñapti*), they merely constitute one; and that one is a conventional designation, not having the true and the conventional as its essence.
Therefore, it is called "middle.
Since the ultimate and the conventional function together,
it is termed "provisional."
Question: Why is that which is neither true nor conventional designated as the "middle," while the true and the conventional are designated as the "provisional"?
Answer: It is by relying on the negation of both [extremes] that one brings to rest the views of the two extremes.
Therefore, it is called "middle.
In reality, neither the ultimate nor the conventional exists; however, for the sake of sentient beings, one forcibly designates and speaks of them as "ultimate" and "conventional.
Thus, the names "ultimate" and "conventional" are merely provisional.
Second, both essence and function are termed "the Middle," because the Middle is the correct meaning;
it possesses that which is neither true nor conventional, as well as that which is both true and conventional.
Because this meaning is fundamentally correct, it is entirely termed "the Middle.
Third, both the ultimate and the conventional, as well as that which is neither ultimate nor conventional, are all provisional.
The reason they are all called "provisional" is that they are all the Tathāgata’s teachings expressed through provisional names.
Therefore, all these are merely provisional designations.

The reason for this is that within the gateway of the Way, neither the ultimate nor the conventional ever truly exist; it is only through provisional designation that the ultimate and the conventional are spoken of.
Therefore, the ultimate and the conventional are provisional;
yet they have never been non-ultimate and non-conventional. To say they are "provisional" is not to say they are non-ultimate and non-conventional.
Therefore, that which is neither real nor conventional is also provisional.
Furthermore, the real and the conventional do not themselves constitute the real and the conventional;
thus, that which is neither real nor conventional is the real and the conventional. Since the real and the conventional are both provisional, [the non-real/non-conventional is likewise so].
Neither the ultimate nor the conventional exists independently; rather, they arise through the ultimate and the conventional.
Because of the ultimate and the conventional, that which is neither ultimate nor conventional is itself also a mere designation.
Question: Since both are equally designations, can they further be combined into a single designation?
Is it by synthesizing the one into the middle?
Answer: Only when the meanings of the ultimate, the conventional, and that which is neither ultimate nor conventional are fully present is it perfectly complete;
only then does it constitute a single, perfect Middle Way.
The true and the conventional are neither true nor conventional; from the very beginning, they are a single, perfect provisional [reality].
Question: When one speaks solely of the true and the conventional, what is the "middle" and what is the "provisional"?
When one directly speaks of that which is neither true nor conventional, what again is the "middle" and what is the "provisional"?
Answer: To speak briefly, it is not the case that the conventional and the ultimate constitute its essence (tǐ), while the conventional and the ultimate constitute its function (yòng).
Within the context where the conventional and the ultimate constitute its function, [it is provisionally established].
The middle [nature] does not have the true or the conventional as its essence.
The reason for making this statement is that one wishes to explain the term "provisional" (*prajñapti*) within the treatise;
therefore, one provisionally establishes essence and function.
Furthermore, this is to counter the view that the ultimate and the conventional are the substance itself;
since there is nothing that is not the substance of the ultimate and the conventional,
it is clarified that the ultimate and the conventional are the functions.
It is not that the non-true and the conventional are themselves the essence;
rather, it is intended to cause one to abandon the dualistic views of the true and the conventional so that one may attain profound awakening.
If one clings to these words and forms a conceptual understanding based on them, the fault is even deeper.
The Master further said:
"To directly designate essence and function is to have no further lingering traces.
The reason for this is that once one speaks of essence and function,"
This is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Since the essence and function of dependent origination are themselves the nature of quiescence (*śāntatā*),
why do you still cling to these words?
Just as it is with the single matter of essence and function,
one must always be conscious of the four modes of conduct— whether moving or still— in relation to the six sense organs.
If one carefully discerns these causes and conditions, then one will know them.
Regarding the four modes of conduct arising from causes and conditions, they have never been either four or not four;
there is no further place for a state of inferiority.
Therefore, one does not give rise to craving or views regarding these four modes of conduct.
Thus, one is constantly in accord with the Way.
The Master further said:
"Whatever is spoken is intended solely to cure the illness."
When the illness subsides, the discourse ends;
it is like hail striking the grass— the grass dies and the hail vanishes—
and one may no longer cling to the words as the final interpretation.
To adhere to words and form interpretations leads back to illness;
one will not attain liberation.
Furthermore, the Master said:
"Since one speaks by observing the mind, speech itself is the non-moving observation.
Having finished this non-moving observation, when has there ever been any speaking?
The Master spoke again:
It is said that words are used to manifest the Way, yet there are no words to which it can be entrusted;
thus one knows that words are not different from the Way. Since there are no words to which it can be entrusted, what Way could possibly be entrusted to words?
Immediately, the mind has nothing whatsoever upon which to rely.
If one further relies on this very non-reliance, then that non-reliance itself becomes a reliance.
It is hoped that those guests of lofty awakening will look toward this profound indication and undergo a single transformation.
Citing one case is sufficient to illustrate all others.
Question: For what reason does the Master establish the "middle-way conventionality" (*madhyama-prajñapti*), and by what reasoning does he then refute that middle-way conventionality?
The answer has already been explained above.
Now, we shall again discuss the meaning of the nature of the causal source (*yul-las byung-ba'i rang-bzhin*).
For this reason, provisional remedies (*upāya*) are established as teachings to treat the specific ailments of partiality.
Therefore, within the clarification of the Middle Way,
one is led to abandon partiality and not cling to the Middle;
the nature departs and does not remain as a mere conventionality.
One must immediately know this:
in partial relinquishment there is nothing to be relinquished;
in the departure of nature there is nowhere to go.
Formerly, there was a scholar in the mountains named Dharma Master Huìjìng.
He said: "When delusion departs, the master of discourse departs;
this departure has no place to which it goes."
Consequently, one abandons partiality and abides in the middle way;
by removing intrinsic nature and establishing the conventional,
one settles the mind in this manner and ultimately does not perceive even a Buddha.
The reason for this is that the Buddha-mind has nothing upon which it relies,
whereas your mind has something to which it is attached;
thus, you are separated from the Buddha.
For what reason can one see the Buddha?
It is for this purpose that [the self] must be refuted.
Furthermore, those who have not yet studied the Three Treatises (Sanlun) must also refute the provisional person within the Middle Way.
Having already harbored an understanding of Sāṃkhya,
you now listen to the Three Treatises and again form an understanding to settle your mind.
Since both are settled within the mind, both are instances of having something attained (*upalabdha*).
How does this differ from the former?
Furthermore, it exceeds others by far.
The reason for this is that previously, one had already obtained the old interpretations of the Sāṃkhya school.
Now, having further acquired new insights from the Three Treatises,
I have added one more perspective.
My teacher said:
This is merely a brief summary;
one could say that the more one's learning expands, the more one's confusion increases.
The intent of the sutras and treatises lies in stilling the mind to reach the fundamental source;
therefore, one is called a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, one stills the mind until there is no longer even stilling.
Regarding what is called "not destroying provisional existence":
for one who realizes the Way, they penetrate the fact that this nature of provisionality is fundamentally the Way itself and need not be destroyed.
Since one would be destroying it if one wished to do so, would that not be destroying the Way?
One must most deeply perceive this meaning.
What is now called "destruction" occurs because [the opponent] does not know that the nature established as provisional has from the beginning been the Way;
thus, they take the Way to be non-Way.
Now, it is merely to cause them to realize that what is not the Way is being taken for the Way;
therefore, it is said that they are "broken," yet in truth, they are not broken at all.
Second, one must further understand that nature itself is merely provisional;
ordinary beings, through their inversions, mistake the provisional for an established nature.
The Buddhas observe that the nature of all things is eternally provisional;
therefore, it is said that all worldly truths are,
for the Tathāgata, eternally the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Third, those who embody the Way know that this Way has never relied upon provisional nature;
provisional nature arises from two conditions.
It is also like how the One Way has never been either true or conventional.
The ultimate and the conventional arise from two conditions.

Fourth, those who follow the stream of scriptural inquiry must recognize that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have internally attained unimpeded contemplation and externally possess boundless discernment.
To speak of the conventional as having intrinsic nature; to speak of intrinsic nature as being conventional;
and to speak of the conventionality of intrinsic nature as being non-intrinsic-nature conventionality.
That which is not a nature is provisionally designated as a nature;
if one clings to a mere fragment of a word,
one loses the perfect meaning and is no longer a student of the Three Treatises.
The Commentary on the Madhyamakaśāstra, Fascicle Two, Part B, is completed.
